questions.q: A note reads: 'chilly, a steady drizzle, a light breeze from the west and a falling barometer.' Counting each element once, the note covers ___ of the five elements of weather.
A newsroom intern drafts four one-line bulletins for a hill town. Which line speaks about exactly one element of weather, with no second element slipping in?
questions.a: Only the first line speaks of a single element, atmospheric pressure. 'Cold drizzle' joins temperature and precipitation, 'damp air and a stiff breeze' joins humidity and wind, and 'hot and sticky' joins temperature and humidity.
o: Atmospheric pressure fell steeply between midnight and dawn.
A cold drizzle kept falling through the whole of the morning.
Damp air and a stiff breeze made the evening unpleasant.
Hot and sticky afternoons are likely to continue all week.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: Atmospheric pressure is the weight of the air above us, felt on the Earth's surface, so it is a different element from wind, which is the movement of air.
Statement 2: Precipitation covers only water that falls as rain; snow, sleet and hail belong to other elements.
Statement 3: A person who notes only how fast the air is moving has recorded just one feature of one element.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 2 is false: precipitation is any form of water that falls from the sky, including snow, sleet and hail. Statement 1 is true (pressure is the weight of air, wind is its movement). Statement 3 is true: wind has two features, speed and direction, and speed alone is one of them.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: A radio station leads its bulletin with one element on each of four days: (i) a July day of non-stop downpour in Mumbai; (ii) a May afternoon of 45 degrees Celsius in still air at Churu; (iii) a day when a cyclone is moving up the Bay of Bengal; (iv) a June afternoon when a hot, dusty loo blows through Lucknow. Which list gives the element the chapter calls dominant on days (i) to (iv), in that order?
questions.a: The chapter pairs rainfall with July, temperature with May, atmospheric pressure with a moving cyclone and wind with a blowing loo. The loo is hot, which tempts one to say temperature, but the chapter names wind for a loo.
o: Precipitation, temperature, atmospheric pressure, wind
Precipitation, temperature, wind, atmospheric pressure
Humidity, temperature, atmospheric pressure, temperature
Precipitation, wind, atmospheric pressure, temperature

questions.q:
A hill town's bulletins. Monday: 29 degrees Celsius, no rain, 1012 mb, wind 10 km/h from the west, humidity 45%. Tuesday: 29 degrees Celsius, no rain, 1004 mb, wind 25 km/h from the west, humidity 45%. Wednesday: 24 degrees Celsius, 12 mm of rain, 998 mb, wind 30 km/h from the north, humidity 85%.
(a) Between Monday and Tuesday exactly two elements changed. Name them.
(b) How many of the five elements changed between Tuesday and Wednesday? Name the feature of the wind that changed besides its speed.
questions.a: (a) Atmospheric pressure (1012 to 1004 mb) and wind (speed 10 to 25 km/h); temperature, precipitation and humidity stayed the same. (b) All five changed: temperature, precipitation, pressure, wind and humidity. Besides speed, the wind's direction changed from west to north.
s: Part (a): atmospheric pressure and wind
Part (b): all five elements; wind direction also changed

questions.q: True or False: Humidity and precipitation are the same element, since both are about water. Give your verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air, while precipitation is any form of water, such as rain, snow, sleet or hail, that falls from the sky. They are two separate elements, so a reading of one does not give the other.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: humidity is water vapour in the air; precipitation is water that falls (rain, snow, sleet, hail)

questions.q: A student models the lowest layer of the atmosphere at a scale of 1 cm for every 1.5 km. Her column for a tropical town is 12 cm tall. Using the chapter's range of 6 km to 18 km for the height of this layer, which pair is right: the height her column stands for, and the shortest column that still stays inside the range?
questions.a: 12 cm x 1.5 km = 18 km, the top of the chapter's range. The lower end, 6 km, needs 6 / 1.5 = 4 cm. Dividing instead of multiplying gives 8 km and 9 cm, and forgetting to convert or multiplying the wrong way gives the other pairs.
o: 18 km, and 4 cm
8 km, and 9 cm
18 km, and 6 cm
18 km, and 9 cm

questions.q: Imran says, 'When a cyclone is moving, atmospheric pressure is the dominant element, so a bulletin need not report the other four elements on that day.' Is he right? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says that in different situations one of the elements is dominant, and it names atmospheric pressure when a cyclone is moving; dominant means it stands out, not that the others vanish. Temperature, precipitation, wind and humidity together with pressure define the weather at a place, so the bulletin still needs all five.
s: Verdict: No
Dominant means one element stands out in a situation; it is not the only one
The five elements together define the weather at a place

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Two towns can both record 30 degrees Celsius at noon and still have different weather.
Reason (R): The weather of a place is defined by temperature, precipitation, atmospheric pressure, wind and humidity together.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A. Weather is the combined state of all five elements, so equal temperature leaves the other four free to differ between the two towns.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.q:
Rina says, 'Weather and atmosphere mean the same thing.'
(a) Using the chapter's definition, state how weather is related to the atmosphere.
(b) A coastal town records 26 degrees Celsius at 7 a.m. and 33 degrees Celsius at 3 p.m. on one day. Can these be two different weathers over the same atmosphere? Give the reason from the definition.
questions.a: (a) The atmosphere is the layer of gases (air) around the Earth; weather is the state of that atmosphere at a particular time and place. (b) Yes. Weather is tied to a particular time as well as a place, so the same town can have a different state of the atmosphere at 7 a.m. and at 3 p.m.
s: Part (a): weather is the state of the atmosphere at a particular time and place
Part (b): yes, because weather belongs to a particular time, so it can differ at one place

questions.q: Kavya's weather card has three entries only: temperature, rainfall and wind (speed and direction). Judge whether the card is enough for each of three users. (i) A ferry captain deciding whether to sail. (ii) A coastal town watching a cyclone approach. (iii) A family deciding whether wet clothes will dry on the line by evening. Where it is not enough, say which element of the chapter must be added and why.
questions.a: (i) Enough on wind: sailors need wind data, and the card gives speed and direction. (ii) Not enough: atmospheric pressure must be added, because it is the dominant element when a cyclone moves and a fall below 1000 mb indicates a depression. (iii) Not enough: humidity must be added, because when the air already holds much water vapour, water evaporates slowly and clothes stay damp.
s: (i) wind is enough for a ferry captain: sailors need wind data
(ii) adds atmospheric pressure
(ii) reason: dominant with a cyclone; below 1000 mb is a depression
(iii) adds humidity
(iii) reason: much water vapour makes evaporation slow

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column I with the element of weather that decides it in Column II.
Column I: 1. The air feels 'heavy' just before a thunderstorm   2. Seeds are carried across a field   3. Wet clothes stay damp on a rainy day because water evaporates slowly   4. Curd takes longer to set in the kitchen
Column II: (a) Humidity   (b) Temperature   (c) Atmospheric pressure   (d) Wind
Choose the correct pairing.
questions.a: A 'heavy' feeling before a storm relates to atmospheric pressure (c); seeds flying are carried by wind (d); slow evaporation on a rainy day is a matter of humidity (a); slow-setting curd points to a fall in temperature (b). The other pairings swap two of these.

questions.q:
A kite club's log for a windy afternoon reads only 'wind: 15 km/h'.
(a) Which feature of the wind is missing from the log?
(b) Name two kinds of people who, according to the chapter, must be aware of wind data, and say why.
questions.a: (a) The direction of the wind (speed and direction are the two features used to describe it). (b) Air pilots and sailors, because the wind has a great influence on flying and sailing.
s: Part (a): direction is missing
Part (b): pilots and sailors, wind greatly influences flying and sailing

questions.q: A bulletin line reads: 'Humidity 92 per cent; precipitation nil.' Which reading of it fits the chapter's meaning of the two elements?
questions.a: Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air; precipitation is water that falls. They are separate elements, so a high humidity with nil precipitation is possible. 92 per cent is not saturation (100 per cent), and neither element is a depth of rain.
o: The air holds much water vapour, but no rain, snow, sleet or hail is falling
The air holds little water vapour, because nothing is falling from the sky
The air is saturated, so rain is bound to fall within the hour
The gauge has measured 92 mm of water collected during the day

questions.q: A student's chart for a town shows 'humidity: 70%' and nothing else. Show why this reading alone cannot tell us whether any precipitation is falling there.
questions.a: Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air, while precipitation is water that falls from the sky as rain, snow, sleet or hail. They are two separate elements measured separately, so the vapour reading does not say whether anything is falling; the chart would also need a precipitation record such as a rain gauge reading.
s: Humidity is water vapour in the air
Precipitation is water that falls, a separate element
So a precipitation record is also needed

questions.q:
On a Shimla morning a student logs: '8 a.m.: rain that has partly frozen. 10 a.m.: small, hard balls of ice bouncing on the road.'
(a) Give the chapter's word for each of the two entries, in order.
(b) Under which single element of weather should both entries be written, and why?
questions.a: (a) Sleet, then hail. (b) Precipitation, because it is any form of water, such as rain, snow, sleet or hail, that falls from the sky.
s: Part (a): sleet then hail
Part (b): precipitation, any form of water falling from the sky

questions.q:
A school in Pune must decide at 6 a.m. whether the 4 p.m. annual-day rehearsal for 300 students is held on the open ground or in the hall, which seats only 120, so the cast would have to rehearse in three shifts. The science club's morning notes read: 'A: 14 mm collected in the gauge between 9 p.m. and 11 p.m. B: wind 35 km/h from the west, forecast to ease to 10 km/h by noon. C: 24 degrees Celsius. D: relative humidity 78%; the sun is out but the ground is still soggy.' The principal wants the ground if it will be dry by 4 p.m.
(a) Name the element of weather that each of the notes A to D records.
(b) In which band does note D fall, and what does that mean for how fast the wet ground can lose water?
(c) The chapter says a greater wind speed makes soil dry faster. What will the forecast easing of the wind do to the drying, and which feature of the wind is the forecast about?
(d) Decide between the ground and the hall, and justify with at least two elements.
questions.a: (a) A precipitation, B wind, C temperature, D humidity. (b) 78% lies in the 60 to 80% band of humid weather, so water evaporates slowly and the ground will dry slowly. (c) It will slow the drying of the soil; the forecast is about wind speed (the direction given is west). (d) The hall, in three shifts: humid air and an easing wind both slow the drying of ground that already received 14 mm, so it may still be soggy at 4 p.m.; the cost is the extra shifts. An outdoor choice earns the mark only if it admits that humid air and the easing wind slow the drying and names the risk accepted.
s: Part (a): precipitation, wind, temperature, humidity
Part (b): humid band, slow evaporation
Part (c): slower drying; wind speed
Part (d): decision tied to at least two elements, with the cost or risk named

questions.q:
A group builds a model of the lowest layer of the atmosphere at a scale of 1 cm for every 3 km of height. They use the chapter's lowest and highest heights for two columns.
(i) How tall is each column?
(ii) Which column belongs to the poles, which to the tropical zone, and why?
(iii) A visitor asks what a 4 cm column would stand for, and whether it must belong to the poles. Answer both questions.
(iv) Name the layer and say what lives and breathes in it.
questions.a: (i) 6 km gives 2 cm and 18 km gives 6 cm. (ii) The 2 cm column is the poles, where cold air contracts; the 6 cm column is the tropical zone, where warm air expands. (iii) 4 cm stands for 12 km, which is inside the 6 to 18 km range; the poles are the thinner end, so a mid-range height need not belong to the poles. (iv) The troposphere, where all land-based plants and animals, including humans, live and breathe.
s: (i) 2 cm and 6 cm
(ii) poles thinner (cold air contracts), tropics thicker (warm air expands)
(iii) 4 cm = 12 km, inside the range
(iii) it need not be the poles, which are the thinner end
(iv) troposphere, where plants, animals and humans live

questions.q: Write three one-sentence entries for a school diary on a winter morning in Shimla: (i) one that records precipitation in a form other than rain, (ii) one that records humidity, and (iii) one that records wind using both of its features. Name the element after each.
questions.a: Any three correct sentences, for example: (i) 'Snow fell from 6 a.m.' (precipitation); (ii) 'The air is full of water vapour and clothes will not dry' (humidity); (iii) 'The wind blew at 15 km/h from the north' (wind: speed and direction).
s: Precipitation entry in a form other than rain, named
Humidity entry about water vapour in the air, named
Wind entry giving both speed and direction, named

questions.q:
On a May day in coastal Odisha a cyclone is moving up the Bay of Bengal. The port barometer read 1002 mb at 6 a.m. and 987 mb at 6 p.m.; the thermometer touched 41 degrees Celsius at noon; the wind at 6 p.m. blew at 60 km/h. A local radio station has 30 seconds for its evening bulletin, so the editor can lead with one element and must squeeze the rest into a closing line.
(a) By how many millibars did the pressure fall in the 12 hours, and what is the average fall per hour?
(b) By the chapter's rule, is 987 mb a depression, and what can such a system become?
(c) The chapter names one element as dominant in May and another when a cyclone is moving. Name both.
(d) Which element should the editor lead with? Decide and justify with the readings.
questions.a: (a) 1002 - 987 = 15 mb, an average of 15 / 12 = 1.25 mb per hour. (b) Yes: a pressure below 1000 mb indicates a depression, which can develop into a storm or a cyclone. (c) Temperature in May, and atmospheric pressure when a cyclone is moving. (d) Lead with atmospheric pressure: a steady fall to 987 mb is the warning of the cyclone for which the coast must prepare, whereas the 41 degrees is a reading people already feel and gives no warning. A lead with temperature earns the mark only if it argues that heat is the greater immediate danger and still puts the pressure fall in the closing line.
s: Part (a): 15 mb; 1.25 mb per hour
Part (b): yes, below 1000 mb; storm or cyclone
Part (c): temperature in May; atmospheric pressure with a cyclone
Part (d): decision justified with the readings

questions.q: A student's project says, 'Instruments have made nature's signs obsolete.' Which sentence of the chapter most directly contradicts her?
questions.a: Only the first sentence says that traditional ways are still in use today. The other three are true in the chapter, but they speak of meteorology, precision and feelings, and none of them says that nature's signs are still used.
o: Even today, many parts of India use traditional ways to predict the monsoon.
Meteorology is the systematic study of weather and its evolution, the basis for forecasting.
Scientists have worked out ways to measure the elements of weather with great precision.
What is cold for one person may be quite pleasant for another, as Krishnan and Amir show.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: A prediction made from the opening and closing of pine cones is meteorology, because pine cones respond to the humidity of the air.
Statement 2: The knowledge of reading nature's signs has been passed down from generation to generation.
Statement 3: Meteorologists can predict only the next few hours; predictions for days or weeks ahead are beyond them.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 is false: meteorology is the systematic study of weather and the basis of forecasting; reading pine cones is a traditional way of reading nature. Statement 3 is false: meteorologists try to predict after a few hours, a few days or even a few weeks. Statement 2 is in the chapter.
o: 2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q: Meera in Leh reads 59 on her old thermometer, which has only the Fahrenheit scale. Her cousin in Chennai reads 20 on a Celsius thermometer. Using the chapter's statement that 15 degrees Celsius is the same as 59 degrees Fahrenheit, who is in the colder place?
questions.a: 59 degrees Fahrenheit is the same temperature as 15 degrees Celsius, and 15 is below 20, so Meera's place is colder. Comparing 59 with 20 directly mixes two scales, but that does not make the comparison impossible once the equivalence is known.
o: Meera, because 59 degrees Fahrenheit equals 15 degrees Celsius, below 20
The cousin in Chennai, because her reading of 20 is smaller than Meera's 59
Neither can be said, because readings on different scales cannot be compared at all
Both are equally warm, because each is simply a reading from a thermometer

questions.q: In the 12 days before last year's first monsoon rain, Dattu noted ants moving their eggs on 7 days and loud frogs on 9 days; on 5 days he saw both. On ___ of the 12 days he saw at least one of the two signs.

Krishnan in Chennai says, 'It is 20 degrees Celsius here and I feel a little cold.' Amir in Kashmir replies, 'It is 9 degrees Celsius here and it is quite pleasant.'
(a) Whose place is warmer?
(b) Why do their feelings not contradict the readings?
questions.a: (a) Chennai, since 20 is higher than 9 on the same Celsius scale. (b) What is cold for one person may be quite pleasant for another, so feelings differ from person to person; the readings on the common scale settle which place is warmer.
s: Part (a): Chennai is warmer, comparing readings on one scale
Part (b): feelings differ between people, so readings, not feelings, are compared

questions.q: Krishnan in Chennai and Amir in Kashmir decide to compare their weather for one week properly. Plan how they will do it, and say what each day's readings will be used for.
questions.a: Each uses a thermometer; both name the scale in use (for example degrees Celsius, noting that 15 degrees Celsius is the same as 59 degrees Fahrenheit if one has a Fahrenheit thermometer); they read at the same time each day; they report numbers, not words like chilly or pleasant, because feelings differ; they put the two sets of readings side by side to compare the two places day by day; the readings can then be used to plan activities, such as what to wear or whether to hold an outdoor event.
s: Uses an instrument at each place
Names a common scale (or the equivalence of the two)
Reports numbers rather than feelings, with the reason
Compares the two places' readings day by day
States a use of the readings, such as planning activities

questions.q: True or False: Meteorologists can predict the weather only a few hours ahead; for days or weeks ahead, only traditional signs are available. Give your verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter says that meteorologists use precise measurements to try to predict how the weather will behave in a region after a few hours, a few days or even a few weeks. Traditional signs are an older, passed-down way, not the only one beyond a few hours.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: meteorologists predict hours, days or even weeks ahead from measured data

questions.q: By his notes, Dattu's saying 'when the ants carry their eggs uphill, heavy rain follows' has held in 9 of the last 10 monsoons. Which statement about the saying is best supported by the chapter?
questions.a: Ants shifting their eggs to higher ground is a natural behaviour that indicates a coming change in weather, and such knowledge is handed down. Meteorology is systematic measurement; the saying gives no number on a common scale. Nothing in the chapter says ants measure pressure or that signs are false.
o: A valuable inherited hint of coming rain, but not a reading another place can compare
It counts as meteorology, because it has been checked against the rains for many years
It must be false, because nothing not measured with an instrument can be true
It shows that ants measure atmospheric pressure and move their eggs when it changes

questions.q: Nisha says, 'Since feelings of cold differ from person to person, only a thermometer reading can be compared between two places, and nature's signs were never of any use.' Is she right? Give reasons.
questions.a: Partly right. She is right that feelings differ, so a reading on an agreed scale is what two places can compare. She is wrong that nature's signs were never useful: the chapter says that observing birds flying low, frogs croaking or pine cones provided valuable information about coming rain or storms, and it is still used to predict the monsoon.
s: Verdict: partly right
What is right: readings on a common scale are needed because feelings differ
What is wrong: nature's signs gave valuable information and are still used

questions.q:
Assertion (A): To compare the weather of two places we need commonly agreed standards of measurement.
Reason (R): What is cold for one person may be quite pleasant for another.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: because feelings differ from person to person, an agreed measure is needed, as with Krishnan in Chennai and Amir in Kashmir.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.q:
Rahul says, 'The ants moving their eggs, the loudly croaking frogs and the pine cones are all caused by the humidity of the air.'
(a) For which of the three does the chapter say the humidity of the air is the driver?
(b) What does the chapter say the ants and the frogs are doing instead?
questions.a: (a) The opening and closing of pine cones: it is a natural mechanism driven by environmental humidity. (b) The ants are shifting their eggs to higher ground, a natural behaviour that indicates an expected change in the weather, especially heavy rain; the frogs croak in expectation of rain.
s: Part (a): pine cones are driven by humidity
Part (b): ants and frogs show behaviour pointing to expected rain

questions.q:
A farmer near Nashik has 5 acres of paddy ready to cut. His father notes that the ants in the yard are carrying their eggs to a high shelf, that the frogs by the well are very loud, and that the pine cones on the roadside trees are shut. The radio forecast, made from measured data, says the next three days will be dry. Cutting now costs 4,000 rupees an acre in hired labour. Cut paddy that lies in the field when it rains loses 10,000 rupees an acre. A tarpaulin to cover the cut paddy costs 1,500 rupees an acre. Waiting three days would raise the labour cost to 5,000 rupees an acre.
(a) Which of the three observations is driven by humidity, and what does it suggest about the air?
(b) What kind of knowledge are the father's observations, and what study produced the forecast?
(c) Find the cost of cutting now and covering all the paddy, and the extra labour cost of waiting.
(d) Decide whether to cut now and cover, cut now without cover, or wait. Justify.
questions.a: (a) The shut pine cones; they close in humid conditions, so the air is humid. (b) Traditional knowledge, read from nature and passed down; the forecast came from meteorology, the systematic study of weather. (c) Cutting and covering: 5 x (4,000 + 1,500) = 27,500 rupees. Waiting: 5 x (5,000 - 4,000) = 5,000 rupees extra. (d) Cut now and cover: the cover costs 7,500 rupees, only 15 per cent of the 50,000 rupees that uncovered cut paddy could lose, and three signs point to rain while the forecast is a prediction, not a certainty. Waiting or not covering earns the mark only if it uses the forecast's precision and states the risk accepted.
s: Part (a): pine cones, humid air
Part (b): traditional knowledge; meteorology
Part (c): 27,500 rupees; 5,000 rupees extra
Part (d): decision weighing signs, forecast and costs

questions.q: The gardener of a school notes that the pine cones in the nursery were wide open at 8 a.m. and tightly shut by 4 p.m. on the same day. What does this suggest about the air around them during the day?
questions.a: Pine cones open in dry conditions to release their seeds and close in humid conditions to protect them. Open at 8 a.m. points to dry air and shut at 4 p.m. to humid air, so humidity rose. They are driven by humidity, not at random.
o: Its humidity rose between morning and afternoon
Its humidity fell between morning and afternoon
It was humid at both times, since pine cones move at random
Its temperature changed, which says nothing about humidity

questions.q: (a) Write a saying, in the form 'When you see ..., expect ...', using any one sign from the chapter. (b) Explain why your saying cannot tell a farmer in another state how much the rain will differ from his own, while a measurement on an agreed scale can.
questions.a: (a) For example: 'When frogs croak loudly, expect rain' or 'When ants carry their eggs uphill, expect heavy rain' or 'When birds fly low, expect rain or storms'. (b) A saying gives only an indication of coming rain and no number on a common scale, so it cannot be compared with another place; a measurement on an agreed scale can.
s: Part (a): a saying using one chapter sign with its weather
Part (b): no number on a common scale, so no comparison

questions.q: Dattu says, 'The frogs are loud tonight, so tomorrow it will rain exactly 40 mm.' Show why none of the nature's signs in the chapter can support the number 40 mm.
questions.a: The signs in the chapter, such as croaking frogs, ants shifting eggs or low-flying birds, only point to coming rain or storms; they say that rain may come, not how much. An amount can be stated only by measuring it with an instrument on an agreed unit, which the signs do not provide, so 40 mm cannot be read from the frogs.
s: Signs only indicate coming rain or storms
An amount needs measurement with an instrument
A number needs an agreed unit that others can compare

questions.q: Dattu has watched ants and frogs for forty years and is right about the rains most years. Asha has spent two years recording temperature, rainfall and pressure at set times every day and now uses the figures to forecast the next few days. Which of the two is practising meteorology, as the chapter defines it?
questions.a: Meteorology is the systematic study of weather and its evolution, the basis for forecasting. Asha measures at set times and forecasts from her data. Dattu's knowledge is valuable, passed-down observation of nature, but it is not measurement. The chapter does not make a weather station a condition.
o: Asha, because she measures the weather systematically and forecasts from her data
Dattu, because forty years of watching is a longer study than two years of readings
Both, because anyone who predicts rain correctly is a meteorologist
Neither, because meteorology needs a weather station with an automatic instrument

questions.q:
Dattu's family has used ants and frogs to read the coming rains for decades.
(a) According to the chapter, how has this knowledge reached them, and where is it still used today?
(b) Name one thing it lacks that a thermometer reading has.
questions.a: (a) It has been passed down from generation to generation, and in many parts of India people still use such traditional ways, especially to predict the arrival of the monsoon. (b) A reading on a commonly agreed scale, which can be compared across places.
s: Part (a): handed down through generations; still used for the monsoon
Part (b): a number on an agreed scale that can be compared

questions.q: A student says, 'Instrument forecasts are scientific, so the elders' sayings about the weather are worthless.' Write a reasoned reply using the chapter, in which you (i) say what the sayings have given, (ii) say whether they are still used, (iii) say what they cannot do that measurement can, (iv) say what meteorology adds, and (v) end with how the two can be used.
questions.a: (i) Birds flying low, ants carrying eggs, frogs croaking and pine cones gave valuable information about coming rain or storms. (ii) The knowledge has been passed down, and in many parts of India it is still used, especially for the monsoon. (iii) A saying gives no reading on a commonly agreed scale, so places cannot be compared, and feelings of cold differ between people. (iv) Meteorology is the systematic study of weather based on precise measurement, and it is the basis for forecasting after hours, days or weeks. (v) They can be used together: sayings as an inherited first hint, measured data for comparison and forecasts.
s: Sayings gave valuable information on rain or storms
Still used today, for example for the monsoon
Cannot give a comparable reading on an agreed scale
Meteorology adds precise measurement and forecasts of hours to weeks
Conclusion: the two can be used together

questions.q:
Lakshmi in Chennai writes that her morning felt chilly and that her thermometer, marked in degrees Celsius, shows 15. Harpreet in Leh writes that his morning felt pleasant and that his old thermometer, which has only the Fahrenheit scale, shows 59. Their cousin Neha in Pune measured 18 degrees Celsius and found it warm. They plan a joint trek and want a single thermometer for the group: one marked only in Celsius costs 250 rupees, and one marked in both scales costs 400 rupees.
(a) Which of the three readings can be compared with another as they stand, with no conversion?
(b) Write Harpreet's reading in Celsius.
(c) Whose mornings were equally cold, and what does this show about the words chilly and pleasant?
(d) Which thermometer should the group buy? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) Lakshmi's 15 degrees Celsius and Neha's 18 degrees Celsius, because both are on the same scale; Harpreet's is on a different one. (b) 15 degrees Celsius, since 59 degrees Fahrenheit is the same as 15 degrees Celsius. (c) Lakshmi's and Harpreet's mornings, both 15 degrees Celsius, although she called hers chilly and he called his pleasant, so such words are feelings that differ between people. (d) The two-scale thermometer is supported, as Harpreet can read the scale he is used to while everyone else compares in Celsius, for 150 rupees more; the Celsius-only one is also acceptable if the group agrees to log everything in Celsius and Harpreet gives up his old thermometer.
s: Part (a): the two Celsius readings
Part (b): 15 degrees Celsius
Part (c): Lakshmi and Harpreet; feelings differ for the same temperature
Part (d): a justified choice that keeps one agreed scale for comparison

questions.q: Write a three-line phone call in which Krishnan in Chennai and Amir in Kashmir exchange temperatures so that each understands the other exactly. One of them must use the Celsius scale and the other the Fahrenheit scale, and the call must use the chapter's pair of equal readings.
questions.a: For example: Krishnan: 'It is 15 degrees Celsius in Chennai.' Amir: 'My thermometer shows 59 degrees Fahrenheit here.' Krishnan: 'Then we have the same temperature, since 15 degrees Celsius is 59 degrees Fahrenheit.' The call names the scale with each number and uses the pair correctly.
s: Krishnan states a reading with its scale (Celsius)
Amir states a reading with its scale (Fahrenheit)
Uses 15 degrees Celsius = 59 degrees Fahrenheit correctly to compare

questions.q: A recording thermometer in Ajmer gave a maximum of 41 and a minimum of 23 degrees Celsius for one day. The next day the range was 4 degrees more than this day's range, and the minimum was 3 degrees lower than this day's minimum. What was the next day's maximum, in degrees Celsius?
questions.a: This day's range is 41 - 23 = 18, so the next day's range is 22. The next minimum is 23 - 3 = 20. The maximum is 20 + 22 = 42. Keeping the old minimum gives 45, using the old range with the new minimum gives 38, and moving the minimum the wrong way gives 48.

questions.q: True or False: For any day, the range of temperature equals twice the difference between the maximum temperature and the mean daily temperature. Give your verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: True. The mean (maximum + minimum) divided by 2 lies exactly halfway between the two, so maximum minus mean is half of (maximum minus minimum). Doubling it gives the range. Check: maximum 34, minimum 18, mean 26, 2 x (34 - 26) = 16 = range.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the mean lies halfway between maximum and minimum, so maximum minus mean is half the range

questions.q: Radha's chart entry for a day in Bhopal reads: maximum 38 degrees Celsius, minimum 41 degrees Celsius. She works out the mean as 39.5. What should her teacher conclude?
questions.a: The maximum is the highest and the minimum the lowest temperature of the period, so the maximum cannot be lower than the minimum. The entry has been swapped or wrongly recorded; the range would come out negative (38 - 41 = -3), which is impossible, and a mean between two swapped values hides the error.
o: The two readings were swapped or wrongly recorded, since a day's maximum cannot be below its minimum
The range of the day was 3 degrees Celsius and the entry is acceptable, because range is the difference of the readings
The entry is fine, because the mean of 39.5 lies between 38 and 41
The thermometer must be digital, as only a digital one can show a minimum above the maximum

questions.q:
A school records (maximum, minimum) in degrees Celsius on three days: (36, 22), (38, 24) and (37, 21).
(a) Find the range of temperature for the whole three-day period.
(b) A student adds the three daily ranges and gets 44. Explain why this cannot be the range for the period.
questions.a: (a) The highest maximum is 38 and the lowest minimum is 21, so the range is 38 - 21 = 17. (b) The range of a period is the highest maximum minus the lowest minimum over that period; the three daily ranges (14, 14 and 16) each cover only their own day, so adding them overcounts. The period's range cannot exceed the gap between the hottest and the coldest reading of all.
s: Part (b): period range is highest maximum minus lowest minimum, not a sum of daily ranges

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: The range of temperature for a day can be found from a thermometer that shows only the temperature at the moment of reading.
Statement 2: A day with a maximum of 34 and a minimum of 18 degrees Celsius has a mean daily temperature of 26 degrees Celsius.
Statement 3: Two days can have the same mean daily temperature and different ranges.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 is false: the range needs the day's maximum and minimum, and an ambient thermometer shows only one reading. Statement 2 is true: (34 + 18)/2 = 26. Statement 3 is true: for example maximum 31, minimum 29 and maximum 40, minimum 20 both have mean 30 but ranges 2 and 20.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
3 only

questions.q: On a day in Jaipur the maximum temperature was 31 degrees Celsius and the mean daily temperature was 25 degrees Celsius. The minimum temperature that day was ___ degrees Celsius.
A report gives a maximum of 36 and a minimum of 24 degrees Celsius for Nagpur. Meena writes the mean daily temperature as 12. What is the right mean, and what did she most probably find instead?
questions.a: The mean is (36 + 24) divided by 2 = 30. Her 12 is 36 - 24, the range. Halving the range would give 6, not 12, and 60 is the sum of the two readings.
o: 30 degrees Celsius; she found the range
30 degrees Celsius; she halved the range
60 degrees Celsius; she found the range
6 degrees Celsius; she found the range

questions.q: Sheela says, 'The mean daily temperature of a day can never be lower than that day's minimum or higher than its maximum.' Test her claim with Day A (maximum 30, minimum 16) and Day B (maximum 36, minimum 30).
questions.a: Yes, the claim holds. Day A: mean (30 + 16)/2 = 23, between 16 and 30. Day B: mean (36 + 30)/2 = 33, between 30 and 36. The mean is the value halfway between the maximum and the minimum, so it always lies between them.
s: Computes Day A mean 23 and checks it lies between 16 and 30
Computes Day B mean 33 and checks it lies between 30 and 36
Verdict: the claim is right, as the mean is halfway between the two

questions.q:
Kiran read her thermometer once at 9 a.m. (24 degrees Celsius) and once at 6 p.m. (28 degrees Celsius), and wrote: 'mean 26, range 4'. The day's recording thermometer showed a maximum of 33 and a minimum of 21 degrees Celsius.
(a) Find the day's true mean and range.
(b) Give the reason why her two readings gave a different range.
questions.a: (a) Mean (33 + 21)/2 = 27 degrees Celsius; range 33 - 21 = 12 degrees Celsius. (b) The range and the mean need the day's highest and lowest temperatures; her two spot readings were not necessarily taken at those moments, so they missed the extremes.
s: Part (a): mean 27 and range 12
Part (b): two spot readings miss the day's maximum and minimum

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The mean daily temperature is the maximum minus the minimum divided by two.
Reason (R): The range of temperature is the maximum temperature minus the minimum temperature.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false: the mean is (maximum + minimum) divided by 2. R is a true definition of range, so the answer is that A is false and R is true.
o: The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.

questions.q:
A city's chart for seven days gives (maximum, minimum) in degrees Celsius: (29, 16), (30, 15), (31, 17), (32, 18), (30, 17), (28, 14), (29, 15).
(i) Find the day with the greatest daily range, and that range.
(ii) On how many days did the mean daily temperature exceed 23 degrees Celsius?
(iii) Find the range for the whole week.
(iv) Find the day with the highest mean daily temperature and say what its range was.
(v) The daily means stay between 21 and 25, yet the weekly range is large. Explain what each number tells us.
questions.a: (i) Daily ranges are 13, 15, 14, 14, 13, 14, 14, so the second day has the greatest, 15. (ii) Means are 22.5, 22.5, 24, 25, 23.5, 21 and 22, so three days exceed 23 (the third, fourth and fifth). (iii) 32 - 14 = 18. (iv) The fourth day, mean 25, with a range of 14. (v) The means lie within a spread of only 4 degrees, so the typical level of the days is steady; the weekly range of 18 shows how far the hottest and coldest readings of the week are apart, which the means hide.
s: (i) second day, 15
(ii) three days
(iii) 18
(iv) fourth day, mean 25, range 14
(v) means steady, range shows the swing between extremes

questions.q: Use this week's chart: maximum temperatures 29, 30, 31, 32, 30, 28, 29 and minimum temperatures 16, 15, 17, 18, 17, 14, 15 degrees Celsius for seven days in order. Which day had the lowest mean daily temperature, and what was it?
questions.a: Daily means are 22.5, 22.5, 24, 25, 23.5, 21 and 22. The lowest is 21 on the sixth day, (28 + 14) divided by 2. The lowest minimum, 14, is not a mean.
o: The sixth day, 21 degrees Celsius
The sixth day, 14 degrees Celsius
The seventh day, 22 degrees Celsius
The first day, 22.5 degrees Celsius

questions.q:
Match each item in Column I with its value in Column II.
Column I: 1. Mean daily temperature of a day with maximum 32 and minimum 20 degrees Celsius   2. Minimum of a day whose maximum is 30 and whose range is 12 degrees Celsius   3. Maximum of a day whose mean is 25 and whose minimum is 19 degrees Celsius   4. Range of a day with maximum 33 and minimum 18 degrees Celsius
Column II: (a) 18   (b) 26   (c) 31   (d) 15
Choose the correct pairing.
questions.a: (1) (32 + 20)/2 = 26, so b. (2) 30 - 12 = 18, so a. (3) the sum of maximum and minimum is 2 x 25 = 50, so the maximum is 50 - 19 = 31, so c. (4) 33 - 18 = 15, so d. The other pairings swap two of these values.

questions.q:
On an unusually steady day in a hill town the thermometer showed the same highest and lowest value, 18 degrees Celsius.
(a) Find the range and the mean daily temperature.
(b) A student says the mean should be 36 because two readings are added. Using the chapter's definition, say where she went wrong.
questions.a: (a) Range 18 - 18 = 0; mean (18 + 18)/2 = 18 degrees Celsius. (b) The mean is the maximum plus the minimum divided by two; she added but did not divide by two.
s: Part (a): range 0 and mean 18
Part (b): the sum must be divided by two

questions.q: A weather chart shows a day with a range of 12 degrees Celsius and a mean daily temperature of 24 degrees Celsius. Find the maximum and the minimum temperature of that day and verify your answer.
questions.a: Maximum + minimum = 2 x 24 = 48 and maximum - minimum = 12, so the maximum is 30 and the minimum is 18. Check: range 12, mean (30 + 18)/2 = 24.
s: Sets up sum 48 and difference 12
Maximum 30 and minimum 18
Verifies both range and mean

questions.q:
The science club of a school in Indore has 800 rupees to buy thermometers for the school roof. Thermometer P has a coloured liquid that rises in a thin tube, shows only the temperature at the moment it is read, and costs 180 rupees. Thermometer Q is digital, records the maximum and minimum of each day, is more precise, and costs 650 rupees. The club's aim is to report the range and the mean of every day for a month. The teacher would also like to know whether the four roof corners differ in temperature.
(a) Which thermometer can give the range of a day, and why can the other not do so on its own?
(b) What does the club lose if it buys four of P to cover the four corners?
(c) Can the club afford one Q and one P together? Show by how much it falls short or has to spare.
(d) Decide what the club should buy and justify.
questions.a: (a) Thermometer Q: the range needs the day's maximum and minimum, which it records; P shows only the present temperature. (b) The recorded maximum and minimum of each day and the extra precision: readings of the four P would depend on someone looking at the right moments. (c) 650 + 180 = 830, which is 30 rupees more than 800, so the club falls short by 30 rupees. (d) Buy Q alone: the stated aim is the range and the mean of every day for a month, which needs recorded maximum and minimum. Four P are supported only if the club gives up that aim for the corners question, since 720 rupees buys no recording; either choice earns the mark if the cost is named.
s: Part (a): Q; P shows only the present temperature
Part (b): loses recorded maximum and minimum and precision
Part (c): 830, short by 30 rupees
Part (d): decision tied to the stated aim, with the cost named

questions.q:
A thermometer on a winter day shows a maximum of 22 and a minimum of 6 degrees Celsius.
(a) Find the range and the mean daily temperature.
(b) The thermometer is later found to read 2 degrees too high at both ends. Say what happens to the range and to the mean when the readings are corrected, with the new values.
questions.a: (a) Range 16, mean 14. (b) Corrected readings are 20 and 4: the range stays 16 because both ends move equally, while the mean falls by 2 to 12 degrees Celsius.
s: Part (a): range 16 and mean 14
Part (b): range unchanged at 16, mean 12

questions.q: Two days in Kota had the following readings: on Day X the maximum was 31 and the minimum 29 degrees Celsius; on Day Y the maximum was 40 and the minimum 20 degrees Celsius. Find the range and the mean daily temperature for each, and justify the statement that 'the mean alone does not describe a day's temperature'.
questions.a: Day X: range 2, mean 30. Day Y: range 20, mean 30. Both days have the same mean, but Day X was steady while Day Y swung from 20 to 40. Hence the range is needed along with the mean to describe the day.
s: Day X range 2 and mean 30
Day Y range 20 and mean 30
Notes the means are equal
Interprets the very different ranges
Conclusion: both statistics are needed

questions.q: A hill station's chart gives (maximum, minimum) in degrees Celsius for four days: Monday (14, 6), Tuesday (16, 10), Wednesday (12, 4), Thursday (19, 8). Find (i) the day with the highest mean daily temperature and that mean, (ii) the day with the smallest range and that range, and (iii) the range for the whole four-day period, saying why it is larger than any single day's range.
questions.a: (i) Means are 10, 13, 8 and 13.5, so Thursday has the highest, 13.5 degrees Celsius. (ii) Ranges are 8, 6, 8 and 11, so Tuesday has the smallest, 6 degrees. (iii) Highest maximum 19, lowest minimum 4: range 15, which exceeds Thursday's 11 because the period's hottest and coldest readings fall on different days.
s: (i) Thursday, mean 13.5
(ii) Tuesday, range 6
(iii) 15, larger because the extremes fall on different days

questions.q:
A school in Pune plans its sports day, with races running from the morning chill into the afternoon. The weather chart for five days gives (maximum, minimum) in degrees Celsius: Day 1 (31, 19), Day 2 (33, 20), Day 3 (31, 21), Day 4 (34, 18), Day 5 (30, 22). The PT teacher wants the day with the lowest mean daily temperature. The school nurse wants the day on which the temperature changes least, and each is ready to defend a different day.
(a) Which day had the greatest range, and what was it?
(b) Find the mean daily temperature of every day and name the day with the lowest.
(c) What is the range of temperature for the whole five-day period?
(d) Which day should the school choose? Decide, name the statistic you rely on and say what you give up.
questions.a: (a) Day 4, with a range of 34 - 18 = 16. (b) Means are 25, 26.5, 26, 26 and 26, so Day 1 has the lowest, 25 degrees Celsius. (c) Highest maximum 34, lowest minimum 18: range 16. (d) Day 5 is supported if the range is relied on: its range of 8 is the smallest and its maximum of 30 the lowest, while its mean of 26 is only 1 degree above Day 1's; what is given up is the lowest mean. Day 1 is supported if the mean is relied on (25, the lowest), at the cost of a range of 12 and a cool 19 degrees morning. Either earns the mark if the statistic and the cost are named.
s: Part (a): Day 4, 16
Part (b): means 25, 26.5, 26, 26, 26; Day 1 lowest
Part (c): 16
Part (d): choice with the statistic relied on and the cost named

questions.q: On a hot afternoon Aditi says the weather feels 'heavy', as it does before a thunderstorm. Which weather reading does the chapter link to that feeling?
questions.a: The chapter says the 'heavy' feeling before a thunderstorm is related to atmospheric pressure. Humidity is a tempting answer, as heavy air feels sticky, but the chapter ties the feeling to pressure.
o: Atmospheric pressure (barometer)
Relative humidity, from a hygrometer
Depth of rainfall, from a rain gauge
Wind speed, from an anemometer

questions.q: A coastal barometer reads 987 mb. Its pressure is ___ mb below the normal pressure at the sea coast.
A harbour's barometer read 1010, 1004, 998 and 991 mb at intervals of six hours. Which statement fits the chapter?
questions.a: 998 mb is already below 1000 mb, so the third reading is the first to indicate a depression, and 991 mb continues the fall. The normal at the coast is around 1013 mb; nothing in the chapter says pressure falls below 1000 mb daily.
o: The pressure was below 1000 mb from the third reading, which indicates a depression that may become a storm
Only the last reading is below 1000 mb, so a depression is indicated only then, and it might become a storm
The fall is about 6 mb per interval, which is slow, and 998 mb is still normal for the coast
Pressure at a harbour is expected to fall below 1000 mb each evening, so the trend gives no warning

questions.q:
A barometer at a hill station reads far lower than the one at a coastal town on the same calm day.
(a) Does this show a depression at the hill station?
(b) Give the reason for the lower reading.
questions.a: (a) No, not by itself; a depression is a dramatic drop in pressure that can become a storm, whereas this low reading is a steady feature of the place. (b) The hill station is higher up, where the air is thinner and presses less.
s: Part (a): no, altitude alone is not a depression
Part (b): thinner air at height gives lower pressure

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: A rain gauge whose cylinder holds water 12 mm deep shows that the area received 12 mm of rainfall.
Statement 2: The atmospheric pressure on the plains or the coast is not always high; it can sometimes drop dramatically.
Statement 3: The pressure at Khardung La, about 650 mb, is more than a third lower than the sea-coast normal of around 1013 mb.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: All three are correct. The depth of water collected is the rainfall; the chapter says pressure on the plains and the coast can drop dramatically; and (1013 - 650)/1013 is about 36 per cent, which is more than a third.
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q: Explain, with the chapter's two pressure figures, why people travelling to a place like Khardung La are advised to make pauses on the way up, and say what the pauses do.
questions.a: The sea-coast normal is around 1013 mb, while at Khardung La, over 5600 m above sea level, the pressure is generally about 650 mb, which is 363 mb lower. At that height the air is thinner, so there is less oxygen for the lungs to take in. With less oxygen getting into the blood, the body works harder and people feel breathless, dizzy or tired. Pauses on the way let the body acclimatise, that is, adjust to the new conditions.
s: Coast about 1013 mb against about 650 mb at the post, 363 mb lower
Thinner air at height
Less oxygen reaches the lungs and blood
Body works harder: breathless, dizzy, tired
Pauses let the body acclimatise

questions.q: True or False: A depression is a place of high atmospheric pressure, so it brings clear weather. Give your verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. A depression, or low-pressure system, is a place where the pressure has dropped, below 1000 mb in the chapter's rule, and it can sometimes develop into a storm or even a cyclone.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: a depression is a low-pressure system that can become a storm or cyclone

questions.q: Four classes keep a month-long rain record. Which class follows every instruction the chapter gives for placing and using a rain gauge?
questions.a: Class A has an open site, a flat surface and a fixed daily time. Class B's gauge tilts, Class C's rain is obstructed by the tree, and Class D reads at no fixed time; each breaks one instruction.
o: Class A: flat stand in the open playground, read at 8 a.m. every day
Class B: gauge clamped on a slanting wall bracket in the open, read at 8 a.m. every day
Class C: gauge on a flat table beneath a thick tree, read at 8 a.m. every day
Class D: flat stand in the open playground, read whenever a student is free

questions.q: Pooja says, 'The pressure at the sea coast is always 1013 mb, so if a barometer by the sea shows 995 mb, the barometer must be faulty.' Do you agree? Explain.
questions.a: No. 1013 mb is the normal value, around which the pressure usually lies. The chapter says pressure can drop dramatically near the coast and below 1000 mb indicates a depression, so 995 mb may be a genuine reading showing a low-pressure system.
s: Verdict: disagrees with the word 'always'
1013 mb is the normal value, not a fixed one
995 mb is below 1000 mb and indicates a depression

questions.q: (a) Give one reason why measuring atmospheric pressure is important. (b) Name one group of people who would use pressure readings and say what they would do with them.
questions.a: (a) A sharp fall in pressure (a reading below 1000 mb) shows a depression, which can develop into a storm or cyclone, so measuring it helps forecasters warn people. (b) Any one with its use, for example weather forecasters, fishermen or sailors deciding whether to put to sea, pilots, or army personnel and trekkers travelling to high places who need to know the air is thin.
s: Part (a): a fall in pressure shows a depression that can become a storm
Part (b): a user group with a sensible use

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A fall of the barometer below 1000 mb at a coastal town warns of a possible storm.
Reason (R): Atmospheric pressure is lowest at the sea coast, so any coastal reading below 1013 mb is a depression.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true: a pressure below 1000 mb indicates a depression, which can sometimes develop into a storm or cyclone. R is false: the pressure is higher near the sea coast and lower as one goes up, and the depression mark is below 1000 mb, not below 1013 mb.
o: The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.q:
At 6 p.m. the district weather office receives barometer readings from two fishing harbours. Harbour A read 997 mb at 6 a.m., at noon and at 6 p.m. Harbour B read 1013 mb at 6 a.m., 1007 mb at noon and 1001 mb at 6 p.m. The office can ask only one harbour to keep its boats back tonight; each harbour's fleet earns about 2 lakh rupees on a sailing night.
(a) Which harbour's latest reading is already below the chapter's depression mark?
(b) At the rate of fall seen, what will Harbour B read at midnight, and will it be below that mark?
(c) What can a depression become?
(d) Which harbour should be asked to keep its boats back? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) Harbour A (997 mb is below 1000 mb). (b) B has fallen 6 mb every six hours, so it will read 995 mb at midnight, which is below 1000 mb. (c) A storm or even a cyclone. (d) Harbour B is supported: its pressure is falling steadily and will cross the mark tonight, so a depression is developing. Harbour A is supported if the answer argues that 997 mb is already below 1000 mb, so a depression is indicated now, even though the pressure is steady. Either earns the mark if the rule, the trend and the risk to the boats are used.
s: Part (a): Harbour A
Part (b): 995 mb, below 1000 mb
Part (c): a storm or cyclone
Part (d): decision using the 1000 mb rule and the trend

questions.q: During a descent from a high camp on a clear day, a mountaineer's barometer rises from 700 mb to 760 mb in two hours. What best explains the rise?
questions.a: Pressure is higher near the sea coast and lower as one goes up into the mountains, so descending raises the reading. A depression is a fall of pressure, a barometer measures pressure not temperature, and the coast has the higher pressure.
o: She is coming down, where the air is thicker and the pressure higher
A depression is forming over the camp, and a depression raises the pressure
The barometer measures temperature, which rises as she goes down
She is moving away from the sea coast, where the pressure is lower

questions.q: A coastal town's barometer shows 650 mb on a calm, ordinary day, and the observer says the pressure is normal for the coast. Show why this cannot be right.
questions.a: The normal pressure at the sea coast is around 1013 mb, and a pressure below 1000 mb already indicates a depression, so a calm, ordinary day cannot go with 650 mb, which is 363 mb below the normal. The chapter gives about 650 mb as the pressure at a very high place such as Khardung La, over 5600 m up, where the air is thin; so the reading is the figure of a high place, and at a coastal town it must come from a faulty instrument or reading.
s: Normal coast pressure is around 1013 mb; below 1000 mb is a depression
650 mb is 363 mb below normal, far from a calm day
650 mb is the figure of a very high place, so the reading is faulty

questions.q: Write a one-line weather bulletin for a coastal town that contains one reading from a rain gauge and one from a barometer, with the barometer reading warning that a storm may be forming. (a) Give the rain-gauge reading with its unit. (b) Give the barometer reading with its unit and say which rule makes it a warning.
questions.a: For example: 'Rainfall 22 mm today; barometer 986 mb.' (a) The rain-gauge reading is a depth in mm. (b) The barometer reading is in millibars and is below 1000 mb, which indicates a depression that can develop into a storm.
s: Part (a): a rain-gauge depth with the unit mm
Part (b): a barometer reading below 1000 mb with the rule that it indicates a depression

questions.q: The sea-coast normal is around 1013 mb, and the pressure at Khardung La is generally about 650 mb. Roughly what percentage of the sea-coast normal is the pressure at Khardung La?
questions.a: 650 divided by 1013 is about 0.64, so about 64 per cent. The 36 per cent figure is how much lower it is, not what it is.
o: About 64 per cent
About 36 per cent
About 50 per cent
About 78 per cent

questions.q: A group must choose a site for its rain gauge from four: (1) the vegetable garden, ringed by tall banana plants; (2) the school terrace, open to the sky, but its surface slopes towards a drain; (3) an open ground with a level raised platform, away from trees and buildings; (4) the top of the compound wall, open but only 10 cm wide, where the wind is strong. Which site should they choose, and why is each of the others unsuitable?
questions.a: The open ground with the level platform: it is open, so nothing obstructs the rain, and flat, so the gauge will not tilt. The garden's tall plants would obstruct the rain; the sloping terrace would make the gauge tilt; the narrow wall top is so exposed to wind that the gauge may topple.
s: Chooses the open ground with the level platform
Garden obstructs rain and terrace slope makes the gauge tilt
Wall top: the gauge could topple in the wind

questions.q:
Class 7B kept a gauge on a flat, open platform for four weeks of seven daily readings each. The weekly totals were: Week 1, 14 mm; Week 2, 35 mm; Week 3, 0 mm; Week 4, 21 mm.
(i) What must the class have done about the site and about the time of reading?
(ii) Find the daily average for each week.
(iii) Which week was wettest, and by how many mm per day did its average exceed the average of the whole month?
(iv) A student says the 0 mm in Week 3 proves the gauge failed. Give the chapter-based reason this does not follow, and one check she can make.
questions.a: (i) Placed the gauge in the open, away from obstructions, on a flat surface that cannot tilt or topple, and read it at the same time every day. (ii) 2, 5, 0 and 3 mm per day. (iii) Week 2, with 5 mm per day; the month's average is 70/28 = 2.5, so Week 2 exceeded it by 2.5 mm per day. (iv) Rainfall varies from week to week, so a dry week is possible and the chapter asks students to comment on the variation; she can check that the gauge was open and level and the funnel was not blocked.
s: (i) open and flat site, same time daily
(ii) 2, 5, 0 and 3 mm per day
(iii) Week 2, 2.5 mm per day above the month's average of 2.5
(iv) rainfall varies, so a dry week is not proof of failure
(iv) a check: gauge open, level, funnel clear

questions.q:
A student's gauge gives daily averages of 2, 5, 0 and 3 mm for four consecutive weeks. She says the gauge must be faulty because the weekly numbers jump about so much.
(a) Is week-to-week variation by itself a fault of the gauge? Give the chapter's reason.
(b) Name two checks on the gauge's placement that would show whether the gauge itself is at fault.
questions.a: (a) No. Rainfall does vary from week to week; the chapter's activity asks students to calculate weekly averages and comment on the variation, not to treat it as a fault. (b) Check that it stands in the open, away from objects that might obstruct rain, and that it is on a flat surface where it will not tilt or topple in the wind (also that it is read at the same time every day).
s: Part (a): variation in rainfall is expected, not a fault
Part (b): two placement checks: open site, flat and steady

questions.q:
A landslide has cut the road to an army post over 5600 metres above sea level, where the pressure is generally about 650 mb. A relief team from the coast must reach the post, because one patient there needs a doctor within 3 days. The usual trek takes 4 days: 2 days of walking and 2 long pauses of one day each. The commander proposes to drop both pauses and arrive in 2 days; the senior doctor wants at least one pause kept.
(a) By how many millibars, and about what percentage, is the post's pressure below the sea-coast normal?
(b) Why is the team likely to feel breathless, dizzy or tired there?
(c) How many days will the trek take if only one pause is kept, and does that meet the patient's limit?
(d) Should the team drop both pauses, keep one or keep both? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) 1013 - 650 = 363 mb, about 36 per cent lower. (b) The air is thinner at that height, so less oxygen reaches the lungs and blood and the body works harder. (c) 3 days, which just meets the 3-day limit. (d) Keep one pause: it still reaches the patient within 3 days and gives some time to acclimatise, which the chapter advises. Dropping both is defensible only if the patient cannot wait until the third day, accepting that the team may arrive unwell; keeping both fails the 3-day limit.
s: Part (a): 363 mb, about 36 per cent
Part (b): thinner air, less oxygen
Part (c): 3 days, meets the limit
Part (d): choice that weighs the 3-day limit against acclimatising

questions.q: At dawn in a hill town, thick fog hangs over the lake and a hygrometer reads 100%. Which statement is supported by the chapter?
questions.a: Air saturated with water vapour is rated at 100%, so the reading is possible. It is the 0%, air with no water vapour at all, that cannot occur in nature. 100% lies above the humid band of 60% to 80%.
o: Saturated air, and such a reading is possible in nature
The reading must be faulty, because 100% cannot occur in natural conditions
The air holds no water vapour, so the weather is dry
The weather is in the usual humid band of 60% to 80%

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: A wind vane has a rotating arm with a pointer at one end and a tail at the other, and its pointer turns in the direction of the wind even in a light breeze.
Statement 2: A wind sock is used only at airfields and never by industries.
Statement 3: Humid weather usually falls between 60% and 80% relative humidity, so a reading of 30% would be called humid.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 is in the chapter. Statement 2 is false: similar socks are used in industries that release ash or gases. Statement 3 is false: 30% lies in the usual dry band of 20% to 40%.
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q: An anemometer's meter counted 120 spins of the cups in a 2-minute period on Monday morning and 150 spins in a 3-minute period on Tuesday morning. Tuesday's count is higher. Which day had the stronger wind?
questions.a: The stronger the wind, the faster the rotation, so the rate matters, not the total over different periods. Monday: 120/2 = 60 spins a minute; Tuesday: 150/3 = 50 spins a minute. Monday's wind was stronger. Direction is not needed to compare speeds.
o: Monday, as 60 spins a minute is faster than 50 spins a minute
Tuesday, as 150 spins is more than 120 spins
Both days, as the cups spun for a whole number of minutes
Neither can be said, as the direction of the wind is not given

questions.q:
Between 2 p.m. and 4 p.m. the cups of an anemometer on a pole spin faster, while the pointer of the wind vane on the same pole does not move. At 6 p.m. the pointer turns from east towards north while the cups spin at the same rate as before.
(a) Describe what happened to the wind between 2 p.m. and 4 p.m.
(b) Describe what changed at 6 p.m.
questions.a: (a) The wind became stronger (its speed rose) but its direction did not change. (b) The wind's direction changed from east towards north; its speed stayed the same.
s: Part (a): speed up, direction unchanged
Part (b): direction changed, speed unchanged

questions.q: A hygrometer gives six readings in one day: 22%, 35%, 41%, 63%, 79% and 85%. The number of readings that fall in the chapter's usual band for humid weather is ___.
Gopal says, 'A greater wind speed makes the soil dry faster, so a farmer should watch the anemometer; the wind direction tells him nothing about the rain.' Is he right? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. The chapter says a greater wind speed will cause the soil to dry faster, so the speed from the anemometer does matter to a farmer. But it also says farmers use the wind direction to predict where rain might come from, so direction does tell him something about the rain, and a wind vane gives it.
s: Verdict: partly right
What is right: greater speed dries the soil faster
What is wrong: farmers use direction to predict where rain may come from

questions.q: A museum's manuscript room reads 72% relative humidity at noon. The curator wants it within the chapter's usual band for dry weather, 20% to 40%. By about how many percentage points must the humidity fall to reach the top of that band?
questions.a: The top of the dry band is 40%, so the fall needed is 72 - 40 = 32 percentage points. 12 is 72 - 60, 52 is 72 - 20 and 8 is 80 - 72, each using the wrong edge of a band.

questions.q: True or False: A wind sock on an airfield and a wind vane are the same kind of instrument. Give your verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: True. The chapter says the wind vane on the tarmac is called a wind sock; like any wind vane it shows the direction of the wind, which pilots use during take-off and landing.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: a wind sock is the wind vane used on the tarmac, and it shows wind direction

questions.q:
A school's anemometer meter counted spins over different periods on five mornings: Day 1, 90 spins in 3 minutes; Day 2, 140 in 4 minutes; Day 3, 100 in 2 minutes; Day 4, 75 in 3 minutes; Day 5, 120 in 5 minutes.
(i) Find the spins per minute on each day.
(ii) Rank the days from strongest to weakest wind.
(iii) Which day had the largest count but was not the strongest, and why?
(iv) On which day would wet soil in a field dry fastest, and why?
(v) The farmer also wants to know where rain might come from. Which instrument and which feature of the wind does he need?
questions.a: (i) 30, 35, 50, 25 and 24 spins a minute. (ii) Day 3, Day 2, Day 1, Day 4, Day 5. (iii) Day 2 has the largest count, 140, but over 4 minutes; its rate of 35 is lower than Day 3's 50, so the longer period inflated the count. (iv) Day 3, because the stronger the wind the faster the rotation and a greater wind speed dries the soil faster. (v) A wind vane, for the wind's direction.
s: (ii) ranking Day 3, 2, 1, 4, 5
(iii) Day 2: longer period, lower rate
(iv) Day 3: strongest wind dries soil fastest
(v) wind vane, direction

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A greater wind speed makes the soil dry faster.
Reason (R): Farmers use the wind direction to predict where rain might come from.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are in the chapter. R says what farmers use direction for; it says nothing about why speed dries the soil, so R does not explain A.
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
The Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
The Assertion is false, but the Reason is true.

questions.q: A factory that releases ash from a tall chimney wants to know, at any moment, in which direction the ash will drift, so that it can warn the houses on that side. Which cheap arrangement serves the purpose?
questions.a: A wind sock is a wind vane that shows the direction of the wind, and the chapter says similar socks are used in industries that release ash or gases. A hygrometer, rain gauge or barometer measures humidity, rain depth or pressure and says nothing about the drift.
o: A cloth wind sock on a pole by the chimney
A hygrometer fixed high on the chimney wall
A rain gauge kept out in the factory yard
A barometer kept in the manager's office room

questions.q:
At the same temperature the relative humidity is 52% in Delhi and 84% in Kochi.
(a) In which city will wet clothes dry faster?
(b) Using the cooling effect of evaporation, explain where sweating cools a person less.
questions.a: (a) Delhi, since the air holds less water vapour and water evaporates faster there. (b) Kochi: when the air already holds much water vapour, sweat evaporates slowly, so the cooling effect of evaporation is smaller and the person feels hotter and stickier.
s: Part (a): Delhi, quicker evaporation in the less humid air
Part (b): Kochi, slow evaporation gives less cooling

questions.q:
At a small airfield near Nashik the ground staff watch a cloth sleeve on a pole and a four-cup instrument on the roof. On Monday the meter showed an average of 40 spins a minute. At 8 a.m. on Tuesday it showed 60 spins a minute, and the sleeve pointed steadily towards the hills. Two flights are planned for 10 a.m.: a trainee pilot's first solo take-off, which can be shifted to Wednesday at no cost, and an air-ambulance flight to carry a patient to Pune, which an experienced pilot is ready to fly.
(a) Name the cloth sleeve and the four-cup instrument.
(b) By what percentage did the spin rate rise from Monday to Tuesday, and what does it show about the wind?
(c) What does the sleeve tell the pilots, and at which two moments of a flight is it used?
(d) Decide what should happen to each of the two flights, and justify.
questions.a: (a) A wind sock and an anemometer. (b) (60 - 40)/40 = 50 per cent higher; the wind became stronger. (c) The direction of the wind, at take-off and at landing. (d) Shift the trainee's solo to Wednesday, since delay costs nothing and the chapter says the wind has a great influence on flying. The air ambulance may go ahead with the experienced pilot, who is told the stronger speed and the direction from the sleeve, because a patient is waiting; grounding both is also acceptable if it is argued that the stronger wind is a risk to a patient in flight.
s: Part (a): wind sock; anemometer
Part (b): 50 per cent; stronger wind
Part (c): direction; take-off and landing
Part (d): reasoned decision for each flight using wind influence on flying

questions.q:
Match each reading in Column I with what it tells in Column II.
Column I: 1. A hygrometer reads 25%   2. A hygrometer reads 100%   3. The meter of an anemometer shows more spins a minute than yesterday   4. The pointer of a wind vane swings round to face the opposite way
Column II: (a) The wind has become stronger   (b) The air is saturated with water vapour   (c) The weather is dry   (d) The direction of the wind has reversed
Choose the correct pairing.
questions.a: 25% is in the dry band (c); 100% is saturated air (b); a higher spin rate means a stronger wind (a); a pointer turning to face the opposite way means the wind's direction has reversed (d). The other pairings swap two of these.

questions.q: A student's table shows three hygrometer readings in school: 24% in the library, 0% in a closed laboratory and 100% on a foggy morning. Show that exactly one of the three cannot be a genuine reading of natural air, and say why each of the other two can be.
questions.a: The 0% reading cannot be genuine: it would mean air containing no water vapour at all, which is impossible in natural conditions. 24% lies in the usual dry band of 20% to 40%, so it is possible. 100% means air saturated with water vapour, which is the top of the scale and can occur, as on a foggy morning.
s: 0% is impossible: no water vapour at all
24% is in the dry band, so possible
100% is saturated air, so possible

questions.q:
Two wet fields lie side by side. The anemometer beside field A averaged 25 km/h during the day, and the one beside field B averaged 8 km/h.
(a) Which field's soil dried faster, according to the chapter?
(b) Does this tell the farmer where tomorrow's rain might come from? Say what he would need instead.
questions.a: (a) Field A: a greater wind speed will cause the soil to dry faster. (b) No. Speed does not show where rain might come from; the farmer needs the wind direction, which a wind vane gives.
s: Part (a): field A, greater wind speed dries soil faster
Part (b): no; direction, from a wind vane, is what predicts where rain may come from

questions.q: Jyotsna is packing for a June school trip to Mumbai. The forecast says 29 degrees Celsius and 84% relative humidity. What clothes would you advise, and how will the humidity affect how she feels? Use the idea of evaporation.
questions.a: Advise light, cool clothes, because 29 degrees Celsius is warm. A humidity of 84% is very high, with the air already holding much water vapour, so water evaporates slowly. Her sweat will dry slowly and the cooling effect of evaporation will be small, so she will feel hot and sticky.
s: Light, cool clothes for the warmth
High humidity means slow evaporation
So sweat cools less and she feels hot and sticky

questions.q:
A museum in Thiruvananthapuram records the relative humidity in its gallery at noon: Monday 45%, Tuesday 58%, Wednesday 70%, Thursday 84%. It holds 21 old palm-leaf manuscripts and paper maps that need a dry environment, and some stone sculptures that do not. Option X: close the windows and run machines in the whole gallery to keep the air dry, about 1 lakh rupees a month. Option Y: sealed dry cabinets, each holding 10 items and costing 25,000 rupees once; the museum would open them for 2 hours every day for visitors.
(a) Which instrument gave the readings, and which of the four readings lie in the chapter's usual humid band?
(b) By how many percentage points did the humidity rise from Monday to Thursday?
(c) How many cabinets are needed, and what is their one-time cost?
(d) Which option should the museum choose? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) A hygrometer; only Wednesday (70%) lies in the 60% to 80% band (58% is below it and 84% above it). (b) 84 - 45 = 39 percentage points. (c) 21 items need 3 cabinets (10 + 10 + 1), costing 3 x 25,000 = 75,000 rupees. (d) Option Y costs less than a single month of Option X, but opening the cabinets for 2 hours daily lets the gallery's humid air in, which defeats the dry environment museums keep. Y is supported if it is argued that the cabinets are opened only when the hygrometer reads in the dry band or for shorter times; X is supported if full protection is worth 1 lakh a month. Either earns the mark if the cost and the protection are both weighed.
s: Part (a): hygrometer; Wednesday only
Part (b): 39 points
Part (c): 3 cabinets, 75,000 rupees
Part (d): decision weighing cost against protection when the cabinets are opened

questions.q:
A museum's hygrometer reads 38% on Monday and 66% on Friday in a room that holds old manuscripts.
(a) Place each reading in the chapter's usual bands.
(b) Which day is the worry for the manuscripts, and what does the chapter say about water in air of such humidity?
questions.a: (a) 38% is in the dry band of 20% to 40%; 66% is in the humid band of 60% to 80%. (b) Friday: museums need to maintain a dry environment to preserve their exhibits, and in humid air the amount of water vapour is already high, so water evaporates slowly.
s: Part (a): dry band and humid band
Part (b): Friday; humid air is not the dry environment museums keep, and evaporation is slow in it

questions.q: On a flat plain, a barometer reads 1008 mb at Town X and 996 mb at Town Y. Using the chapter's idea of wind: (i) say in which direction the air moves between the two towns; (ii) say which town may be under a depression and by what rule; (iii) name the instrument at Town Y's airfield that shows the direction of the wind and say what a pilot uses it for; (iv) say how a farmer near Y uses wind direction; (v) say what a stronger wind there would do to a wet field.
questions.a: (i) Wind is the movement of air from high to low pressure, so the air moves from X towards Y. (ii) Y: its pressure is below 1000 mb, which indicates a depression. (iii) The wind sock, a wind vane on the tarmac; the pilot uses the wind direction at take-off and landing. (iv) A farmer uses the wind direction to predict where rain might come from. (v) A greater wind speed will cause the soil to dry faster.
s: (i) from X (high) towards Y (low)
(ii) Y, below 1000 mb
(iii) wind sock; direction at take-off and landing
(iv) direction predicts where rain may come from
(v) greater wind speed dries the soil faster

questions.q: True or False: A cyclone forecast that gives two days' notice is useful even though the storm is not yet near, because the time lets the local government mobilise resources and prepare. Give your verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: True. The chapter says accurate predictions help people be ready and let local governments mobilise resources and prepare for disasters, for example by evacuating a coastal area; that preparation needs time before the cyclone arrives.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: predictions let governments mobilise resources and prepare beforehand

questions.q: A forecast issued at 6 a.m. on Monday says a cyclone will reach a district's coast at 6 p.m. on Wednesday. Moving everyone from the coastal villages to relief camps takes 36 hours. By when must the order to move be given for the move to be finished by landfall?
questions.a: Landfall is 60 hours after the forecast. Working back 36 hours from 6 p.m. on Wednesday gives 6 a.m. on Tuesday. An order at 6 p.m. on Tuesday leaves 24 hours, one at 6 p.m. on Monday gives 48 hours, and one at 6 a.m. on Wednesday leaves only 12.
